01 / Context
The design challenge

The existing flow is excellent at one thing: getting from A to B.

Its two-station structure is direct and easy to scan. The challenge was to support intermediate stops without turning every simple booking into a complex route-building task.

Current mental modelA → B

OpportunityWhere should an optional stop live without competing with the primary task?
Design principle
Keep the direct trip as the default. Reveal complexity only when the traveller asks for it.
02 / Interaction model
The route is the interface

One visible sequence, from entry to exit.

Instead of treating each station as an isolated field, the concept turns the form into a route. Every added stop enters the same visual sequence and inherits controls that match its role.

+OptionalAdd stops
2FinishChoose exit
✓ReviewSee route & fare
03 / Key decisions
Interaction decisions

Familiar enough to trust.
Clear enough to use.

01

Make the route visible

A single vertical path connects entry, stops, and exit. Travellers can understand where a new stop belongs before choosing it.

02

Reveal controls progressively

The original two-station flow remains the default. Waypoint controls appear only after “Add a stop,” keeping routine bookings lightweight.

+Add a stopOptional
03

Prevent route errors early

Duplicate stations are flagged before fare review. Reorder and remove actions sit beside the stop they affect.

!
Station already selectedChoose another stop
04 / Interface anatomy
Designed for orientation

Each control answers one question.

  1. Where am I starting?A fixed origin anchors the route.
  2. What happens on the way?Optional stops can be added, reordered, or removed.
  3. Where am I ending?A distinct square marker closes the sequence.
  4. What will this journey cost?Route, duration, stops, and illustrative fare appear together.
